```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  # The vignette downloads data from GitHub
  eval = curl::has_internet()
)
```

StatsBomb makes part of its data freely available in the
[StatsBomb Open Data](https://github.com/hudl/open-data) repository. It covers
around 4,000 matches, such as the FIFA World Cups of 2018 and 2022, the UEFA
Euros of 2020 and 2024, Lionel Messi's La Liga matches and several women's
competitions. Some matches also have StatsBomb 360 data.

The `sb_open_*()` functions download this data without credentials and return
tibbles with the same structure as the functions that access the paid API
(`sb_get_*()`), so the same code works with both sources.

| Open data function | Paid API equivalent | What it returns |
|---|---|---|
| `sb_open_competitions()` | `sb_get_competitions()` | Competitions and seasons available |
| `sb_open_matches()` | `sb_get_matches()` | Matches of one or more competitions/seasons |
| `sb_open_events()` | `sb_get_events()` | Events of one or more matches |
| `sb_open_lineups()` | `sb_get_lineups()` | Lineups of one or more matches |
| `sb_open_360()` | `sb_get_360()` | 360 freeze frames of one or more matches |

## Terms of use

The open data is provided under the
[StatsBomb Public Data User Agreement](https://github.com/hudl/open-data/blob/master/LICENSE.pdf):

- any published analysis must **credit StatsBomb** as the data source and use
  the StatsBomb logo, available in its [media pack](https://statsbomb.com/media-pack/);
- the data **cannot be redistributed or used commercially**.

For this reason the package does not include any data: it is always downloaded
from the official repository. The first `sb_open_*()` call of each session
shows a reminder of these terms.

```{r setup}
library(kickoff)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

## Competitions

`sb_open_competitions()` lists every competition and season available.

```{r competitions}
competitions <- sb_open_competitions()

competitions |>
  select(competition_id, season_id, competition_name, season_name, match_available_360)
```

The column `match_available_360` is filled in when the season has 360 data:

```{r competitions-360}
competitions |>
  filter(!is.na(match_available_360)) |>
  select(competition_name, season_name)
```

The `competition_id` and `season_id` of a season are what you need to get its
matches. Filter the competitions by name:

```{r world-cup}
world_cup_2022 <- competitions |>
  filter(competition_name == "FIFA World Cup", season_name == "2022")

world_cup_2022 |>
  select(competition_id, season_id, competition_name, season_name)
```

## Matches

`sb_open_matches()` takes a data frame with the columns `competition_id` and
`season_id`, usually filtered from `sb_open_competitions()`. Each row is a
competition/season, so you can get several of them at once.

```{r matches}
matches <- sb_open_matches(world_cup_2022)

matches |>
  select(
    match_id, match_date, competition_stage.name,
    home_team.home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team.away_team_name
  ) |>
  arrange(match_date)
```

Nested fields of the JSON are flattened into columns separated by a dot, such
as `home_team.home_team_name` or `competition_stage.name`. The column
`match_status_360` says whether the match has 360 data.

```{r final}
final <- matches |>
  filter(competition_stage.name == "Final")

final |>
  select(match_id, home_team.home_team_name, away_team.away_team_name, match_status_360)
```

## Events

`sb_open_events()` takes a vector of match ids or a data frame with the column
`match_id`, such as the output of `sb_open_matches()`. It returns one row per
event, with the column `match_id` added at the start.

```{r events}
events <- sb_open_events(final)

dim(events)
```

Each event has a type (`type.name`) and, depending on the type, its own
columns with a prefix, such as `pass.*`, `shot.*` or `carry.*`:

```{r event-types}
events |>
  count(type.name, sort = TRUE)
```

Fields that hold arrays are kept as list columns. The most common are
`location` and the end locations of passes, carries and shots, which hold
`c(x, y)` coordinates on a 120 x 80 pitch:

```{r locations}
events$location[[10]]
```

### Shots

As an example, here are the shots of the final with their expected goals
(xG). Period 5 is the penalty shootout, so it is left out.

```{r shots}
shots <- events |>
  filter(type.name == "Shot", period < 5) |>
  mutate(
    x = vapply(location, `[`, numeric(1), 1),
    y = vapply(location, `[`, numeric(1), 2)
  )

shots |>
  group_by(team.name) |>
  summarise(shots = n(), goals = sum(shot.outcome.name == "Goal"), xg = sum(shot.statsbomb_xg))
```

```{r shot-map, eval = curl::has_internet() && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
library(ggplot2)

shots |>
  mutate(goal = shot.outcome.name == "Goal") |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, size = shot.statsbomb_xg, colour = team.name, shape = goal)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 60, xmax = 120, ymin = 0, ymax = 80, fill = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 102, xmax = 120, ymin = 18, ymax = 62, fill = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 114, xmax = 120, ymin = 30, ymax = 50, fill = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16)) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(60, 120)) +
  labs(
    title = "Shots in the 2022 World Cup final",
    size = "xG", colour = NULL, shape = "Goal",
    caption = "Data: StatsBomb"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

StatsBomb coordinates are always relative to the team in possession, which
attacks from left to right, so the shots of both teams are on the same side of
the pitch without any transformation. The y axis is reversed because the
coordinates start at the top-left corner of the pitch.

## Lineups

`sb_open_lineups()` returns one row per team and match. The players are in the
list column `lineup`, which can be expanded with `tidyr::unnest()`:

```{r lineups}
lineups <- sb_open_lineups(final)

lineups |>
  select(match_id, team_id, team_name, lineup)
```

```{r lineups-players, eval = curl::has_internet() && requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE)}
players <- lineups |>
  tidyr::unnest(lineup)

players |>
  select(team_name, player_name, player_nickname, jersey_number, country.name)
```

Each player has the list column `positions`, with the positions played and the
time on the pitch in each one. Players without positions did not play.
Expanding it shows the starting lineups and the substitutions:

```{r positions, eval = curl::has_internet() && requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE)}
positions <- players |>
  select(team_name, player_name, positions) |>
  tidyr::unnest(positions)

positions |>
  filter(start_reason == "Starting XI") |>
  select(team_name, player_name, position, from, to, end_reason)
```

## 360 frames

`sb_open_360()` returns one row per event with 360 data. Not every match has
it: check `match_status_360` in the output of `sb_open_matches()`.

```{r frames}
frames <- sb_open_360(final)

frames
```

Each row has:

- `event_uuid`: the event id, which matches the column `id` of the events;
- `visible_area`: the polygon of the pitch visible in the broadcast footage,
  as a vector `c(x1, y1, x2, y2, ...)`;
- `freeze_frame`: a data frame with the players visible at the moment of the
  event, with their `location` and whether they are a `teammate` of the actor,
  the `actor` themselves or a `keeper`.

The frames are joined to the events by `event_uuid` and `id`. As an example,
here is the freeze frame of Ángel Di María's goal:

```{r di-maria}
goal <- shots |>
  filter(shot.outcome.name == "Goal", player.name == "Ángel Fabián Di María Hernández")

goal_frame <- frames |>
  filter(event_uuid == goal$id)

freeze_frame <- goal_frame$freeze_frame[[1]] |>
  mutate(
    x = vapply(location, `[`, numeric(1), 1),
    y = vapply(location, `[`, numeric(1), 2),
    player = case_when(actor ~ "Shooter", teammate ~ "Teammate", keeper ~ "Keeper", TRUE ~ "Opponent")
  )

visible_area <- matrix(goal_frame$visible_area[[1]], ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  setNames(c("x", "y"))
```

```{r di-maria-plot, eval = curl::has_internet() && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
ggplot(freeze_frame, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(data = visible_area, fill = "grey90") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 120, ymin = 0, ymax = 80, fill = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 102, xmax = 120, ymin = 18, ymax = 62, fill = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("segment", x = goal$x, y = goal$y, xend = 120, yend = 40, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = player), size = 3) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title = "Di María's goal (36'), 2022 World Cup final",
    subtitle = "Players visible at the moment of the shot. Grey area: visible pitch",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Data: StatsBomb 360"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

## Several matches at once

All `sb_open_*()` functions accept several matches or competitions and
download them in parallel, combining the results in a single tibble. The
column `match_id` identifies the match of each row.

```{r several}
knockout <- matches |>
  filter(competition_stage.name %in% c("Semi-finals", "Final"))

knockout_events <- sb_open_events(knockout)

knockout_events |>
  count(match_id)
```

Matches without data, such as a match without 360 data or an id that does not
exist, return no rows and generate a single warning listing them:

```{r warning}
frames <- sb_open_360(c(3869685, 12345678))

unique(frames$match_id)
```

An events file is around 3 MB, so downloading whole competitions can take a
while. The number of simultaneous downloads can be changed with
`options(statsbomb.max_active = )` (default is 5).

## Differences from the paid API

The open data files are exported from the StatsBomb API, so the column names
are the same as in the `sb_get_*()` functions. However, some data is not
included:

- **matches** come without attendance and collection status columns;
- **events** come without the On-Ball Value (OBV) columns and other derived
  columns, such as `is_transition` and `possession_directness`;
- **lineups** come without formations, height and weight;
- **360 frames** come without the 360 metrics, such as `line_breaking_pass`;
- **player and team stats** and the **player mapping** are not available.

Code written for the open data works with the paid API data, which only adds
columns. The opposite is not always true: code that uses, for example, the OBV
columns needs the paid API.
